question: Why is a dime smaller than a nickel?
notes: Narration v5 (new goblin ending). Times are seconds into voice.mp3, taken from words.json. Each scene is one stop on the vertical paper strip; the strip scrolls down to the next scene just before its start. 'paint' lists where the red-lead paint lands and the word it lands on. Art ids name files in art/ (PNG line drawings, traced to SVG). Positions are left to the layout. Real US coins: dime 17.9 mm, nickel 21.2 mm, so keep that ratio whenever both coins appear. The three words of the Kupfernickel line were timed from the waveform (Whisper skipped them).

scenes.line: Why is a dime smaller than a nickel, when it's worth twice as much?

art.desc: A dime and a nickel lying side by side, true size ratio, simple line drawing with no readable lettering

scenes.line: Blame a Civil War panic, a man with a nickel mine, and a goblin.

art.desc: A mine entrance with an ore cart and a man in a top hat seen from behind (no face)
A small mischievous mine goblin, original design, crouched and grinning

scenes.layout_note: Three small vignettes on one stretch of strip; the paint hops between them.

scenes.line: Dimes were silver, and ten cents of silver is small.

art.desc: A balance scale with one small dime in the pan

scenes.line: Then the Civil War hit. People hoarded gold and silver, and stores gave change in postage stamps.

art.desc: A jar of coins being lowered into a hole in the ground
A hand passing a postage stamp across a shop counter as change

scenes.line: Congress wanted coins of cheap metal. And nearly all the nickel mined in America belonged to one man. Joseph Wharton.

art.desc: The US Capitol with its dome still in scaffolding (it was finished in 1866)
The top-hatted man from scene 2, now standing on a heap of ore, seen from behind or in silhouette (stylized, no real likeness)

scenes.line: In 1866 came the first five-cent nickel. Cheap metal, so its size was up to Congress. A committee bumped up the weight, officially to make an even five grams. Conveniently, that took more nickel.

art.desc: A 19th-century coin press stamping out a big coin
A committee table with a balance scale on it; one pan gets a weight added and tips
Ore pouring into the press hopper

scenes.line: The silver left the dime in 1965. The size stayed.

paint.on: the dime, then drains out of it, leaving only the ink outline at the same size

scenes.line: Wharton made millions on nickel, and in 1881 he founded a business school. The Wharton School.

art.desc: A generic 1880s university gate and building, no real crests or lettering

scenes.line: And the goblin? German miners kept digging up ore that looked like copper, but gave none. So they blamed a goblin, and named the ore after him.

art.desc: Two 1600s Saxon miners at copper-looking ore, the goblin peeking from a crack
The goblin on his own (reuses the scene 2 drawing)

scenes.beat_note: A short, still beat: the name and its meaning. No other text on screen.

scenes.line: When a chemist found a new metal inside that ore, he kept the goblin's name.

art.desc: The goblin perched on top of a nickel coin

paint.on: the goblin, then it slides down onto the coin

scenes.beat_note: The payoff: the picture says the coin carries the goblin's name, so the narration doesn't have to. Hold a beat after 'name'.

scenes.line: And why does the dime have ridges, but not the nickel? That's another story.

art.desc: Close-up of a dime's ridged edge next to a nickel's smooth edge
